nameStory: The peppered moth gets its name from the speckled, salt-and-pepper pattern found on the wings of its most common form. Like freshly ground black pepper scattered on a light surface, these moths display a beautiful mix of light and dark speckles that help them blend perfectly with tree bark.
description: The peppered moth is a medium-sized night-flying moth with wings that span about 1.5 to 2 inches across. Most peppered moths have pale wings decorated with fine black speckles and spots, though some individuals can be much darker or almost entirely black. These nocturnal visitors are active from late spring through summer, resting during the day with their wings spread flat against tree trunks where their coloring provides excellent camouflage.

idTips.label: Wing pattern
idTips.description: Wings display a distinctive salt-and-pepper speckled pattern with fine black dots and lines scattered across pale grayish-white background, feeling papery and delicate to the touch

idTips.label: Resting posture
idTips.description: Sits with wings held horizontally flat against tree bark during daylight hours, body pressed tight to the surface with no gap underneath

idTips.label: Wing size
idTips.description: Medium-sized with wingspan of 1.5 to 2 inches, about the size of a silver dollar when wings are fully spread

idTips.label: Color variation
idTips.description: Can range from heavily speckled light gray to nearly solid black (melanic form), with the dark forms feeling slightly thicker and more velvety

idTips.label: Antennae
idTips.description: Males have feathery, branched antennae that feel soft and fuzzy, while females have thinner, thread-like antennae

habitat: Peppered moths are found throughout New England's deciduous and mixed forests, particularly where birch, oak, and maple trees provide ideal resting spots. They're commonly seen in suburban areas with mature shade trees, parks, and woodland edges. Look for them on light-colored tree bark, especially birch trees where their camouflage works best.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late May, often found resting on tree trunks during warm afternoons. This is when mating activity peaks and they're most likely to be spotted during daylight hours.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity from June through August when adults are most numerous and active at night around porch lights and outdoor lighting. Caterpillars are actively feeding on tree leaves during this time.
seasonality.fall: Second generation adults may appear in early fall, though numbers are typically lower. Caterpillars pupate in the soil, preparing for winter.
seasonality.winter: Pupae overwinter in the soil beneath host trees. No adult moths are active, but this is when the next generation is developing underground.

funFact: The caterpillars of peppered moths are master disguise artists that can actually sense the color of the twig they're sitting on through their skin and change their body color to match it perfectly — like having built-in mood ring technology that works as camouflage!
confusionNotes: Peppered moths are most easily confused with other geometer moths, but their distinctive speckled pattern and medium size help distinguish them. Remember: if it looks like someone sprinkled pepper on pale wings and it's resting flat against bark during the day, you've likely found a peppered moth.
contextualKnowledge: The peppered moth is famous in biology textbooks as a classic example of evolution in action, particularly the increase in dark-colored moths during the Industrial Revolution when tree bark became soot-covered. This made the peppered moth one of the most studied insects in the world for understanding natural selection.
compareHints: While peppered moths are the only Biston species commonly found in New England, they can be distinguished from other geometer moths in the region by their specific speckled pattern and medium size. Most other geometers are either much smaller, lack the distinctive pepper-like speckling, or have more geometric patterns on their wings rather than the organic, scattered dots of the peppered moth.
